after.problem: Compute the arc length of $y=\frac{1}{8}{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ for $x\in [1,4].$
after.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{1}{8}{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x,$ $a=1,$ and $b=4.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{4}x-\frac{1}{x}
$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{1}{4}x-\frac{1}{x})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{16}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{16}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+\frac{16}{{x}^{2}}+8} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{(\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}=\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{4x}$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{x}{4}+\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{1}{8}{x}^{2})|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)+\frac{1}{8}(4)^{2}]-[\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+\frac{1}{8}(1)^{2}] \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡4+2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\frac{1}{8} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡4+\frac{15}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: The length of a curve $y=f(x)$ is given by ${\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.$ Which of the following could be  an equation for this curve?
after.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We're given that 

$$
L={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Comparing the above with the arc length formula, we see that we must have

$$
[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}=\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}\,⟹\,{f}^{′}(x)=\pm \frac{1}{1-x}.
$$

Integrating the above equation with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\pm \int \frac{1}{1-x}\text{ d}x \\  & =\pm (-\operatorname{ln}⁡|1-x|)+C \\  & =\pm \operatorname{ln}⁡(1-x)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given options, the only one that has the required form is $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-x)+7.$

The length of a curve y=f(x) is given by ∫01/21+1(1−x)2dx. Which of the following could be an equation for this curve?

a
y=ln⁡(x+1)−1
b
y=11−x+2
c
y=1(1−x)2
d
y=ln⁡(1−x)+7
e
y=−11+x
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The arc length of a curve y=f(x) between x=a and x=b can be found using the formula L=∫ab1+[f′(x)]2dx.

We're given that

L=∫01/21+1(1−x)2dx.

Comparing the above with the arc length formula, we see that we must have

[f′(x)]2=1(1−x)2⟹f′(x)=±11−x.

Integrating the above equation with respect to x, we get

f(x)=±∫11−x dx=±(−ln⁡|1−x|)+C=±ln⁡(1−x)+C.

From the given options, the only one that has the required form is y=ln⁡(1−x)+7.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option d. For f(x)=ln(1-x)+7, f'(x)=-1/(1-x), giving exactly the stated arc-length integrand √(1+1/(1-x)²). Option b, the deliberately incorrect submission, instead gives [f'(x)]²=1/(1-x)⁴.

content.knowledge_point: Identifying a Possible Curve Given Its Arc Length As an Integral
content.problem: The length of a curve $y=f(x)$ is given by ${\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.$ Which of the following could be  an equation for this curve?
content.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We're given that 

$$
L={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Comparing the above with the arc length formula, we see that we must have

$$
[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}=\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}\,⟹\,{f}^{′}(x)=\pm \frac{1}{1-x}.
$$

Integrating the above equation with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\pm \int \frac{1}{1-x}\text{ d}x \\  & =\pm (-\operatorname{ln}⁡|1-x|)+C \\  & =\pm \operatorname{ln}⁡(1-x)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given options, the only one that has the required form is $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-x)+7.$

after.problem: Compute the arc length of $y=\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3/2}$ for $x\in [0,3].$
after.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between two points where $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula:

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3/2},$ $a=0,$ and $b=3.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=4\sqrt{x}
$$

Substituting ${f}^{′}(x)=4\sqrt{x}$ to the formula for the arc length, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+[4\sqrt{x}]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+16x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate this integral using the substitution $u=1+16x.$ Then, $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{16}\text{d}u.$

We also need to compute new limits:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 3 \\ u & 1 & 49\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{49}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{16}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{16}{\int }_{1}^{49}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{16}{[\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}]|}_{1}^{49} \\  & =\frac{1}{24}({49}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{343-1}{24} \\  & =\frac{57}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: The length of a curve $y=f(x)$ is given by ${\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+36{e}^{6x}}\,\text{d}x.$ Which of the following could be  an equation for this curve?
after.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that 

$$
L={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+36{e}^{6x}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Comparing the above with the arc length formula, we see that we must have

$$
[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}=36{e}^{6x}\,⟹\,{f}^{′}(x)=\pm 6{e}^{3x}.
$$

Integrating the above equation with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\pm 6\int {e}^{3x}\text{ d}x \\  & =\pm 2{e}^{3x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given options, the only one that has the required form is $y=2{e}^{3x}+1.$
